# The control: what a keyword search returns

The brief says an agent should only work because the content was structured, and that
if a keyword search would have got you the same answer you should aim higher. This is
the other arm of that experiment, run against the same clause texts the knowledge base
is built from, with ordinary tf-idf ranking. Reproduce with:

```bash
npm run ask -- --baseline "how long must I keep automatically generated logs"
```

```

Keyword search over the same clauses
  "how long must I keep automatically generated logs"

  0.2763  EU AI Act Art. 19 — Automatically generated logs
          Providers of high-risk AI systems shall keep the logs automatically generated by their high-risk AI systems, to the extent such logs are under their c…
  0.2763  EU AI Act Art. 26(6) — Deployer duty to keep automatically generated logs
          Deployers of high-risk AI systems shall keep the logs automatically generated by that high-risk AI system to the extent such logs are under their cont…

What the ranking cannot answer, however it is tuned:
  · Do these two clauses contradict each other, or is the second one just also relevant?
  · Which of them binds me — am I the provider here, or the deployer?
  · Is this obligation in force yet, and from which date?
  · Has anyone decided what to do where they collide, and who was it?

Each of those is a relationship between documents. A flat index of the same
documents does not hold relationships, so no amount of ranking produces them.
Run --profile <slug> --no-llm for the answers.
```

## What the three runs show

The first query finds the two AI Act clauses and scores them **identically**. Ranking
cannot break that tie, because which one binds you is not a property of either text —
it depends on whether you are the provider or the deployer.

GDPR Art. 5(1)(e) does not appear at all. It is the clause that makes the answer wrong
if you ignore it, and it is invisible here because it never says *logs*: it says
*personal data*. The second query finds it and pushes the AI Act clauses down instead.

So the two halves of the answer live under different vocabularies, and finding both
requires already knowing both exist — which is the question you were asking.

The third query asks about the conflict directly and returns one clause. The conflict
is not in any document. It is a relationship between two of them, and a flat index of
documents has nowhere to put a relationship.
